To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Five Factor Model (FFM) is the most empirically validated model of general personality and that the ICD and the DSM personality disorder categories are shifting to the FFM model.

the Five Factor Model is a robust and empirically validated model of personality structure, the Five Factor Model has been applied successfully to the study of personality pathology, the Five Factor model is the predominant model for the classification of personality pathology in both the DSM 5 and ICD 11, and the Five Factor Model of personality pathology is a promising model that has already demonstrated clinical utility.

the FFM is a robust, well-validated model of general personality that offers the opportunity for an integrative understanding of the structure of normal and abnormal personality across basic personality science and clinical psychiatry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development, validation, and application of the FFM model of personality structure.
the development of the FFM as a framework for the conceptualization, classification and assessment of personality disorder.
the development and validation of the FFM as the organizing framework for the classification and assessment of the ICD/DSM personality disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the network approach is the most promising approach to psychopathological research and practice.
the FFM is a promising model for the classification of personality disorder, and it is a model that should be further investigated and developed.
the FFM is a promising model for the classification and assessment of personality disorders but that the empirical support for the model is far from conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FFM has been the most empirically supported model for the organization of personality traits.
the FFM offers a superior approach for conceptualizing the ICM and DSM personality disorders.
the FFM is not a perfect model of personality structure, nor is the ICD or DSM model perfect for the classification and assessment of personality disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FFM offers an opportunity for a more comprehensive and integrative understanding of the structure and function of personality across the fields of personality science and clinical psychiatry.
